common_name: Issho-no-Haru Azalea (Rare Fukurin-Patterned White-and-Pink Satsuki Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Issho-no-Haru is an uncommon Satsuki azalea cultivar whose name translates roughly as 'spring together,' referring to the mix of white and pink flowers it carries at once.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, mulching to keep the shallow root system cool and evenly moist. Issho-no-Haru is a rare Satsuki azalea cultivar from Japan's long bonsai and collector tradition, carrying the fukurin color pattern in which some flowers open white and others open pink on the same plant, every bloom marked with red spotting on the upper lobe. Its dark green, glossy foliage is notably dense and holds up well to the repeated shearing typical of Satsuki maintenance after bloom. As with other Satsuki selections, flowering comes later than most Kurume and Southern Indica azaleas, typically in late spring to early summer, and the plant's compact habit suits both container culture and bonsai training. Water deeply during dry spells and prune only right after flowering, since this later-flowering type sets next year's buds soon after bloom ends.

common_name: Juko Azalea (Influential Medium-Pink Satsuki Parent Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Juko is a long-established Satsuki azalea cultivar noted for medium pink flowers and for being a parent of numerous later Satsuki sports.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, mulching to keep the shallow root system cool and evenly moist. Juko is one of the most influential cultivars in the Satsuki azalea lineage, bearing medium pink flowers on a plant that is relatively fast-growing by Satsuki standards, with small dark green leaves set off by comparatively large blooms. Its genetic importance shows in the number of distinct sports it has produced over the decades, including the well-known two-tone sport Karenko, making Juko a useful reference point for understanding Satsuki breeding history. Like other Satsuki cultivars, it blooms later in the season than most Kurume and Southern Indica azaleas, and its mounding form works well as a low border shrub or container specimen in addition to bonsai training. Water deeply during dry spells and prune only right after flowering, since buds for the following year set soon after bloom ends.

common_name: Kaho Azalea (White Satsuki Azalea with Pink Selfs and Stripes)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Kaho is one of the most widely grown Satsuki azalea cultivars, prized for its mainly white flowers that also appear as solid pink selfs or pink-and-white stripes on the same plant.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, mulching to keep the shallow root system cool and evenly moist. Kaho is a twiggy, dense, spreading-to-rounded Satsuki azalea bred from Rhododendron indicum and R. simsii stock, grown for its showy, funnel-shaped, wavy-petaled flowers about 3 inches across that open mainly white but also show solid pink and pink-and-white striped variations on the same bush. Its notably small, lance-shaped to elliptic leaves and compact growth habit have made it one of the most popular Satsuki cultivars for bonsai training, especially in the UK and Europe. Like other Satsuki selections, it flowers later than most Kurume and Southern Indica azaleas, typically from May into June. Water deeply during dry spells and prune only right after flowering, since this later-flowering type sets next year's buds soon after bloom ends.

common_name: Gyoten Azalea (Ruffled Pink Sport of Kaho Satsuki Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Gyoten is an old Satsuki azalea cultivar and sport of Kaho, grown for its large, frilly-edged pink flowers in varied shades with occasional striping.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, mulching to keep the shallow root system cool and evenly moist. Gyoten arose as a sport of the popular Satsuki cultivar Kaho and is grown mainly for its large, ruffled, frilly-edged flowers that range across different shades of pink, with occasional stripes breaking up the color. It belongs to a long line of older Satsuki cultivars valued specifically for their ruffled, namiuchi-style petal form rather than flat or rounded lobes. As with its parent and other Satsuki selections, flowering comes later in the season than most Kurume and Southern Indica azaleas, typically in late spring to early summer. Water deeply during dry spells and prune only right after flowering, since this later-flowering type sets next year's buds soon after bloom ends.

common_name: Suisen Azalea (Star-Shaped Red-Variegated Satsuki Parent Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Suisen is one of the most important modern Satsuki azalea breeding parents, grown for its thick-petaled, star-shaped flowers variegated with red on a white background.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, mulching to keep the shallow root system cool and evenly moist. Suisen is a Satsuki azalea cultivar with thick, star-shaped petals showing a strong mix of red variegation over a white ground, with a fairly prominent central blotch. It is regarded as one of the most widely used parent cultivars in modern Satsuki breeding, having contributed its flower patterning to a large number of later named varieties, even though its own growth habit is considered only average for bonsai purposes compared with its flower display. Leaves are somewhat larger and rounder than many traditional Satsuki cultivars. As with other Satsuki selections, it flowers later than most Kurume and Southern Indica azaleas, typically in late spring to early summer. Water deeply during dry spells and prune only right after flowering, since next year's buds set soon after this later bloom period ends.
sources: The Azalean (Azalea Society of America journal)

common_name: Kinpai Azalea (Rare Multi-Color Star-Shaped Satsuki Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Kinpai is an uncommon Satsuki azalea cultivar grown for its variable, multi-color, five-point star-shaped flowers.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, mulching to keep the shallow root system cool and evenly moist. Kinpai is one of the rarer Satsuki azalea cultivars in collector circles, noted for single, five-point star-shaped blooms whose coloring varies considerably from flower to flower on the same plant, ranging from solid light pink or solid coral pink to white-centered blooms edged in coral, buff, or reddish-orange, sometimes flecked with darker pink spotting. This unpredictable, multi-color display makes each blooming season a little different and adds to the cultivar's appeal among Satsuki collectors. As with other Satsuki selections, flowering comes later than most Kurume and Southern Indica azaleas, typically in late spring to early summer. Water deeply during dry spells and prune only right after flowering, since next year's buds set soon after bloom ends.

common_name: Kobai Azalea (Rose-Red White-Variegated Satsuki Azalea, 'Red Plum')

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Kobai, whose name means 'red plum' in Japanese, is a Satsuki azalea cultivar grown for its rose-red flowers broken by distinct white variegated areas.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, mulching to keep the shallow root system cool and evenly moist. Kobai takes its name, meaning 'red plum,' from its rose-red flowers, which carry distinct white variegated patches rather than a uniform solid color, giving the bloom a painted, two-tone look typical of many Satsuki cultivars. It is established enough in the Satsuki lineage that at least one later cultivar, Kiyoka, is recorded as a seedling raised from it, underscoring its place in Satsuki breeding history. Flower size and shape otherwise follow the typical Satsuki range of single blooms with rounded, overlapping lobes. As with other Satsuki selections, it flowers later than most Kurume and Southern Indica azaleas, typically in late spring to early summer. Water deeply during dry spells and prune only right after flowering, since next year's buds set soon after bloom ends.

common_name: Gettoku Azalea (Large Ruffled White Pink-and-Salmon-Striped Satsuki Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Gettoku (also spelled Getsutoku) is a tetraploid Satsuki azalea cultivar grown for its very large, ruffled, wavy-petaled flowers variegated with pink and salmon stripes over white.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, mulching to keep the shallow root system cool and evenly moist. Gettoku, also spelled Getsutoku, is a tetraploid Satsuki azalea cultivar known for very large, single, wavy-edged flowers that appear in numerous color variations, from solid pink or salmon to white heavily striped with pink and salmon, often with the ruffled namiuchi petal texture associated with several older Satsuki lines. Its medium, bushy, spreading growth habit is a bit looser than some ultra-dwarf Satsuki cultivars, but it has been used successfully as breeding stock behind some of the Robin Hill azalea hybrids. As with other Satsuki selections, flowering comes later than most Kurume and Southern Indica azaleas, typically in late spring to early summer. Water deeply during dry spells and prune only right after flowering, since next year's buds set soon after bloom ends.
sources: Nuccio's Nurseries Satsuki and Satsuki Hybrids catalog
